note.text: Nationalisation transfers privately owned enterprise assets or interests into public ownership through the applicable process. Possible aims include strategic control, service access or coordination. It differs from regulating a private business, subsidising it or merely changing its managers. A transfer may involve acquisition costs and continuing financing obligations. The name of the policy does not establish its outcome: efficiency, access and accountability depend on implementation and circumstances. This lesson uses hypothetical transfers, not an assertion about a current Cameroonian policy or compensation rule.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to explain an ownership transfer to the state and assess possible purposes and costs. Builds on: public, private and mixed ownership. Leads to: privatisation as a movement in the opposite ownership direction.

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: A fictional authority acquires ownership interests in an existing private enterprise to pursue a stated service goal. The enterprise still requires workers, maintenance and oversight. A separate example in which the authority sets quality rules but buys no interest is regulation, not nationalisation. A partial holding must be described accurately rather than called complete ownership.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Identify what ownership changed, who paid or financed it in the model and what goal was stated. Evaluate outcomes with evidence instead of assuming the goal has already been achieved. An ownership percentage alone does not reveal every legal control right in a real enterprise.

cards.idea: Distinguish these features before judging a business.
example: nationalisation: a transfer from private to public enterprise ownership.
strategic-control aim: an intention to direct an activity considered important by public authorities.
acquisition cost: resources required to obtain ownership in the stated transfer.
implementation risk: the possibility that the chosen ownership policy fails to achieve its aims.

cards.idea: Use the stated case evidence to identify the economic feature.
example: The fictional authority acquires an existing private enterprise interest.
The stated policy seeks more public direction over a key service.
The fictional purchase uses public funds that have alternative uses.
Weak oversight can undermine the proposed service improvement.

cards.idea: Explain a consequence instead of assuming every option has the same effect.
example: nationalisation: A regulation need not transfer ownership.
strategic-control aim: An objective must be distinguished from evidence of results.
acquisition cost: Funds used to acquire an interest are not simultaneously available for every alternative.
implementation risk: Management, incentives and accountability still affect performance.

questions.prompt: In an invented enterprise with {total} identical voting shares, public authorities acquire {state} shares. What percentage of these shares do they hold?

misconceptions.explain: That is the remaining private share, not the public holding.
That is the fraction; multiply by one hundred for a percentage.

solution: Public share percentage = public shares / total shares × {100}.
